item.text:
The flow has three distinct stages: checking credentials, resolving a live session, and adding the workspace membership needed for authorization.

The submission starts in `LoginForm` in `src/app/(auth)/login/login-form.tsx`. Its `useActionState` callback reads email, password, and `rememberMe` from `FormData`, then validates them with `loginSchema` from `src/schemas/auth.ts`. The shared `emailSchema` in `src/schemas/common.ts` validates and lowercases the email; login requires a nonempty password. Invalid input becomes field errors. Valid input goes to the Server Action `loginAction` in `src/actions/auth/login.ts`, which repeats validation on the server.

`loginAction` first calls `consumeRateLimit` from `src/lib/rate-limit.ts`, then calls `login` in `src/server/services/auth-service.ts`. That service performs another rate-limit check before checking credentials. These checks use different anonymous organization keys, so they consume two separate buckets. `login` calls `findUserByEmail` in `src/server/repositories/user-repository.ts`, then `findPasswordHash(user.id)`. The normal `User` type deliberately excludes the password hash.

`verifyPassword` in `src/lib/hash.ts` checks the stored `scrypt:<saltHex>:<keyHex>` value. It normalizes the supplied password with NFKC, derives a 64-byte key using scrypt and the stored salt, and compares it with `timingSafeEqual`. An unknown email and an incorrect password both throw “Those credentials did not match.” Exceptions are converted into an `ActionResult` by `toActionResult`; the form displays the returned error.

After successful verification, `login` calls `createSessionToken` in `src/server/services/session-service.ts`. This generates 32 random bytes encoded as base64url and sets an expiry 30 days ahead. It calls `hashToken` in `src/lib/hash.ts` to produce a SHA-256 digest, then passes that digest to `createSession` in `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts`.

The new database row, defined by `sessions` in `src/server/db/schema/users.ts`, contains a generated session ID, user ID, token hash, expiry, creation/update timestamps, and `activeOrgId: null`. The raw token is not stored in the database. Signing in creates a session; it does not create a user, workspace, or membership.

Back in `loginAction`, `resolveSession(token)` hashes the raw token and retrieves its corresponding `SessionPrincipal`. That type, defined in `src/types/member.ts`, contains only `userId`, `email`, `activeOrgId`, and `expiresAt`. The action calls `setSessionCookie` in `src/lib/session.ts`, handing the raw token to the browser in the `taskflow_session` cookie. The cookie is HTTP-only, uses `SameSite=Lax`, applies to `/`, expires with the session, and is secure in production. The action’s response body contains the principal and a submission timestamp, rather than the token or password hash. Although the form submits `rememberMe`, the implementation always uses the same 30-day lifetime.

When the successful result reaches `LoginForm`, its effect calls `router.push(props.next)`. The login page in `src/app/(auth)/login/page.tsx` supplies that destination through `safeDestination`, allowing paths beginning with `/` while rejecting `//` and external URLs; the default is `/orgs`. The page also calls `getSessionPrincipal` before showing the form and redirects immediately if the visitor already has a live session.

On the subsequent navigation, the browser sends the cookie. `proxy` in `src/proxy.ts` checks protected paths for a nonempty session cookie. If it is missing, it redirects to `/login?next=...`. Cookie presence alone lets the request proceed; the proxy does not verify the token against the database.

The actual signed-in check happens through `getSessionPrincipal` in `src/lib/session.ts`. It calls `getSessionToken`, which reads the cookie using Next’s asynchronous `cookies()`, then calls `resolveSession`. That calls `findSessionByTokenHash` in `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts`, which joins the session row to its user and rejects missing or expired sessions. `getSessionPrincipal` additionally checks that the returned expiry is strictly in the future. Thus a later request reconstructs identity from the opaque token and current database records. There is no token refresh or extension in this path.

`Layout` in `src/app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` uses that check and redirects to `/login` when it returns `null`. The session endpoint’s `GET` in `src/app/api/auth/session/route.ts` uses the same check, returning the principal fields or an unauthorized response.

If the destination is `/orgs`, `Page` in `src/app/(dashboard)/orgs/page.tsx` calls `listOrganizationsForUser` in `src/server/services/organization-service.ts`, backed by `listOrgsForUser` in `src/server/repositories/organization-repository.ts`. Exactly one organization causes an immediate redirect to `/${org.slug}`; multiple organizations produce a chooser.

At the workspace URL, `Layout` in `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/layout.tsx` retrieves the principal, resolves the organization with `resolveOrgBySlug`, and calls `resolveActorForOrg` in `src/server/services/session-service.ts`. That function looks up the organization and calls `findMember(org.id, principal.userId)` in `src/server/repositories/member-repository.ts`. It requires a live membership with status `"active"`, then constructs an `Actor` containing `{ userId, orgId, role }`, verifies the organization with `assertOrgScope` from `src/lib/tenant.ts`, and updates the membership’s last-seen timestamp. A missing organization or unusable membership results in `notFound()` in this layout.

This is where bare identity becomes authorization context: **`SessionPrincipal` identifies the signed-in user; `Actor` adds their current role in the workspace addressed by the URL.** The role is fetched from membership rather than embedded in the cookie. Workspace access through this slug-based path also does not require the newly created session’s `activeOrgId` to be populated.

The workspace layout then builds a feature context with `buildFlagContext` in `src/server/services/feature-flag-service.ts` and evaluates it with `snapshotFlags` in `src/lib/feature-flags.ts`. It loads projects, unread notifications, and quota checks in parallel, then passes the organization, actor, flags, and quota checks into `OrgProvider` in `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/_components/org-provider.tsx`. That seeds the client context defined in `src/hooks/org-context.tsx`.

`DashboardShell` in `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/_components/dashboard-shell.tsx` renders the sidebar and top bar, and uses `can` to decide whether to show “New project.” `AppSidebar` in `src/components/domain/nav/app-sidebar.tsx` calls `visibleNav` from `src/config/nav.ts` on `SIDEBAR_NAV` and `SETTINGS_NAV`. `visibleNav` recursively filters entries by their feature flag and required permission.

Those permissions ultimately run through `can` and `explain` in `src/lib/permissions.ts`: reject a different organization first, allow a platform-staff bypass, consult `ROLE_MATRIX` and `ROLE_RANK`, then consider ownership exceptions. Consequently, viewers get basic reading navigation, activity requires at least member, feature-flag management requires admin, and billing requires owner. Flag-dependent entries also require the corresponding flag.

Workspace pages and mutations enforce these rules on the server as well. For example, the overview `Page` in `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/page.tsx` calls `loadTenantContext` from its `_lib/tenant-context.ts`. That resolves the organization, obtains an actor through `getActor` in `src/lib/actor.ts`, checks scope, and evaluates flags. The page uses `can(actor, "org:manage_billing", ...)` before loading billing information. Services such as `listProjects` in `src/server/services/project-service.ts` independently call `assertOrgScope` and `assertCan`. Organization-scoped Server Actions use `withAction` in `src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts` to validate input and resolve an actor from the request before invoking their handler. The browser’s role-aware sidebar therefore reflects the same permission machinery that guards server operations.
